summary:
Delta State stands under Nigeria's national framework: same-sex conduct has been criminal across the country since 1916, and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed in January 2014, criminalises all forms of same-sex union with a maximum federal penalty of 14 years' imprisonment. The statute reaches beyond unions to cohabitation between same-sex partners, public shows of a same-sex amorous relationship, the operation of gay organisations, and participants and guests at same-sex weddings. Section 217 of the Criminal Code makes male gross indecency a felony carrying three years' imprisonment. The death penalty is confined to the twelve northern Shari'a states, where male sodomy is punishable under state Zina provisions. No state-specific protective statute exists in Delta.

Delta has a dated record of active enforcement. In June 2018 Nigerian police arrested more than 100 party-goers at a hotel in Asaba on charges that they were gays and lesbians, and by July 2018 those detainees were facing homosexuality-related charges in court. On 27 August 2023 officers from the Ekpan Division in Uvwie Local Government Area raided Teebolus Hotel on Refinery Road, Ekpan, at 9 pm and arrested 67 suspects for allegedly conducting and attending a same-sex wedding ceremony between Daniel Pius, 22, and Maxwel Ohwonohwo, 20. Delta State Police Command spokesman DSP Bright Edafe said the raid followed a confession by a male cross-dresser that he belonged to a gay club travelling to a gay marriage ceremony; the suspects fled on the officers' arrival, 67 were chased and arrested, and drugs and gay marriage ceremonial dresses were recovered. Edafe said efforts continued to arrest fleeing members for possible prosecution. One suspect alleged he was sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated.

The United States Department of State 2023 human rights report, cited in the UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025, records that on the same date police in Delta State raided a 'white party' organised by the LGBTQI+ community and detained more than 200 individuals, alleging the event was a same-sex wedding; some civil society representatives disputed that account. The Home Office note confirms the national framework under which Delta stands and documents these Delta-specific enforcement incidents, while noting that state-level documentation is thin, which does not demonstrate safety.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression carries exposure. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and six months after the killing no suspects had been charged. Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to six months' imprisonment without the option of a fine and held in a maximum-security prison in Lagos; press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion, and an October 2024 investigative panel found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice, as reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Shari'a law in northern states.
tangentialFactors:
Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. A human rights lawyer based in Warri, Delta State, quoted in the UK Home Office note, reports that kito victims under-report for fear of prosecution, so predatory assault against LGBTQ+ people in the state is under-recorded relative to its incidence.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement nationally. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the 2014 statute as a weaponised law producing a climate of hostility independent of its text, and Wikipedia's overview records nationwide patterns of arrests, raids and vigilante violence relevant to a traveller in Delta.

Delta's enforcement incidents are frequently framed together with drug allegations, as in the Ekpan hotel raid where recovered drugs were listed alongside ceremonial dresses, which broadens the charges available to officers and the exposure of anyone present.
localsOnly:
Residents of Delta State are subject to the same national statutes as visitors, with no state-level protection: the 2014 Act, Section 217 of the Criminal Code and the wider criminalisation of same-sex conduct apply to them directly, and no state-specific protective statute exists. Defendants arrested in the state have proceeded to court, including the more than 100 Asaba detainees who by July 2018 were facing homosexuality-related charges and the 67 individuals charged after the August 2023 Warri raid, a case known as the 'Warri 67'.

Residents who are victims of predatory assault face a reporting dilemma documented by a Warri-based human rights lawyer: kito victims under-report for fear of prosecution under the same laws that criminalise their conduct. Incarcerated residents have no guaranteed placement by gender identity; placement between male and female sections has been left to prison authorities' discretion, and an October 2024 panel found that one such placement violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act.
outOfScopeNotes:
The detention figures for 27 August 2023 in Delta State are not reconciled across sources: the Daily Post account records 67 arrests at Teebolus Hotel in Ekpan, while the United States Department of State 2023 human rights report, as cited by the UK Home Office, records more than 200 individuals detained at a 'white party' on the same date, with civil society representatives disputing the police characterisation of the event as a same-sex wedding. Whether these describe one incident counted differently or two separate actions is unresolved in the sources available here.

Whether the proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here. Outcomes of the 'Warri 67' prosecutions and of the Asaba cases after July 2018 are not sourced. State-level documentation for Delta is thin, and no sourced material addresses Delta-specific rules on identity documents or gender markers, visa and entry screening, restroom or facility access, healthcare or transition-related care, hate-crime protection, or partner and marriage recognition; the absence of such material is not evidence of permissiveness.
